name: Uma Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for agreeing to this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm Uma, I'm 27, and I live with my girlfriend Priya in a rented flat near the ring road. She's a home care worker, so between us we earn enough to get by and not much more. I work on the packing lines at Northfield Frozen Foods, we make frozen pizzas, about forty thousand a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day on the line look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the flow-wrapper, which is the machine that seals each pizza in plastic, and the case packer after it that drops them into boxes. Most of my day is fixing small stops: a film roll runs out, a pizza goes in crooked, the sensor sees a shadow and stops everything. I've only been there ten months and I still call the engineer more than I should. But I love working out why a machine stopped, and on my breaks I ask an AI chatbot what the fault codes mean, which is half how I've learned anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, well, that's a bit of a letdown, I was finding it useful. At work people would rib me about it, because I'm the one always on my phone asking it things. Online I'd say the tools are still handy for learning, even if they didn't change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it's fine for me. I'd still use it as my tutor, and the line would still need people to keep it running. My problem would be the same as now, which is that I'm on the lowest grade and the engineers' jobs are where the money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the free online lessons on PLCs, the little computers that control the machines, about an hour a night. I'd ask my supervisor, Grant, again about shadowing the maintenance team on Fridays. And I'd keep pushing the union rep to get the company to pay for an apprenticeship scheme, because right now it's just people who already know someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bored by it, if I'm honest. I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships go to people who already know someone. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year two spots came up in maintenance. One went to the plant manager's nephew and one to a guy whose dad works in stores. I'm not saying they're bad, but nobody even put up a notice, and there's women on the line who'd have gone for it in a heartbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How tight is money, month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. I have maybe a week's worth of money in the bank at any point. Priya's hours change a lot, so some months we're fine and some months we're eating pasta every night until payday.

S0.say: She'd say it's a bit of a letdown because she was finding AI useful, and that the tools are still handy for learning. Co-workers would tease her for always asking her phone things.
S0.think: She thinks nothing much changes for her: she keeps using AI as a tutor and the line still needs people. Her real problem stays the same, being on the lowest grade while the money is in engineering.
S0.do: Keeps doing about an hour a night of free online lessons on machine controllers and asks her supervisor again to shadow maintenance on Fridays. Presses the union rep for a company-paid apprenticeship scheme that's openly advertised.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little bored; she likes things moving.
S0.quote: Last year two spots came up in maintenance. One went to the plant manager's nephew and one to a guy whose dad works in stores.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is already teaching herself with AI and sees it as a ladder, so a plateau mildly disappoints her. Her anger is about unfair access to training, not technology. She frames her progressive views through who gets chances on the shop floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance, but only if the workers get trained, not just the managers. I'd be saying it loud at union meetings: robots coming in should mean apprenticeships going out. Online I'd post about how I learned fault-finding with a chatbot, to show anyone can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's actually good for me. The packing lines will get more robots, and someone has to keep the robots running, and that person could be me if I move fast. The risk is I'm still learning and the company hires someone from outside instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask Grant straight out to move me onto the new robot cell when it comes, even as a helper. I'd sign up for the evening industrial maintenance course at the college, which I'd pay off monthly, maybe forty a month. If Northfield wouldn't move me, I'd apply to the robot supplier itself, because they need technicians to install the things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, actually. A bit nervous about the money, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay forty a month. Where does that come from, with a week's money in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop my streaming subscriptions and walk to work instead of taking the bus, that's about forty right there. Priya would grumble about the TV. But she'd get it, she's always telling me to aim higher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs. Okafor on the topping line, she's been putting pepperoni on pizzas by hand for fifteen years. A robot does that now at other plants, I've seen the videos. She's terrified of computers, so I'd want the union to make sure she gets a real choice, maybe the quality checking job, not just a goodbye.

S1.say: She'd say this is the workers' chance only if they get trained too, and push the union for apprenticeships whenever robots arrive. Online she'd share how she learned fault-finding with a chatbot.
S1.think: Privately she thinks it's good for her, since someone has to keep the new robots running and it could be her if she moves fast. The risk is the company hiring a trained outsider first.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor in the first month to place her on the new robot cell, even as a helper. Enrols in an evening industrial maintenance course at about forty a month, paid by cutting streaming and bus fares, and applies to the robot supplier if her employer won't move her.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, a bit nervous about money.
S1.quote: Someone has to keep the robots running, and that person could be me if I move fast.
S1.fieldNote: This is the only picture she welcomes outright, and her plan is quick and specific. Her concern shifts to older colleagues with less appetite for change. She funds her training through small cuts rather than borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, right now, that companies can't just switch everyone off. A tax on robots, money straight to the people who lose work. I'd be helping organise, not just turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my whole plan breaks. If AI can do almost any work and the robots can fix each other, then maintenance tech isn't a safe place either. I'd have spent a year learning to look after machines that don't need me, and I'd have no savings to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still keep learning, but I'd stop paying for the course and use the free stuff. I'd sell anything that's worth something, which is basically my bike and an old laptop. I'd put my energy into the union, helping write a demand for a guaranteed income, and I'd try to pick up weekend shifts with Priya's agency, because people will still want a human for care, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and kind of cheated. Like I ran to the train and the doors shut in my face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work might be safe 'for a while'. Why only a while?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Priya says they're already testing robots that help lift people out of bed. I think people would still want a person to talk to. But I don't actually know, and I'd be guessing about something I don't understand yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya the night you found out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'Well, I picked the wrong ladder.' And then I'd make a joke so she didn't worry. Then later I'd lie awake doing sums on my phone.

S2.say: She'd call for emergency rules, a tax on robots and money going straight to displaced workers, and would help organise rather than just attend.
S2.think: She believes her plan to become a maintenance technician falls apart if robots can fix each other. She'd have spent a year learning for a job that disappears, with no savings behind her.
S2.do: Switches to free learning, stops paying for the course, and sells her bike and old laptop. Helps the union draft a demand for a guaranteed income and picks up weekend care shifts through her partner's agency.
S2.feel: Scared and cheated, like reaching the train as the doors close.
S2.quote: I'd say, 'Well, I picked the wrong ladder.' And then I'd make a joke so she didn't worry.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI hits the adaptive worker in a specific way: her chosen escape route closes too. She doesn't freeze; she pivots to care work and organising within days. She openly says she doesn't know if care work would stay human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, and I'd want the union and the government to plan it together. I'd keep showing people at work how to use the AI tools, because the more of us who understand them, the harder we are to fool. Online I'd keep posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32. I think I'd get a few good years out of the maintenance route, three maybe, while the robots still need humans to install and fix them. After that I don't know, but by then I'd have some savings and a skill people pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course in the first year and go for the robot cell job straight after. Once the pay goes up, I'd save as much as I can, maybe a hundred a month, so we've got a real cushion. And I'd help set up a training group at the union, where people teach each other the AI tools on lunch breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd feel like I was doing something. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the more workers understand the tools, the harder they are to fool. Fooled how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like when management says a new machine needs fewer people, and nobody can check. If I can read the spec sheet and ask the AI what it really does, I can tell the union rep, actually, this still needs two operators. Knowing how it works is power in that room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your plans with Priya that would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about getting a place of our own one day. In five years, with this coming, I don't think I'd want a mortgage. I'd rather keep renting and be able to move if the work moves.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough if the union and government plan together now. She'd keep teaching co-workers AI tools, arguing that workers who understand them are harder to fool.
S3.think: She expects a few good years in maintenance while robots still need human installers and fixers. After that she's unsure, but she'd have savings and a paid skill by then.
S3.do: Completes the maintenance course in year one and moves straight to the robot cell job. Saves around a hundred a month once her pay rises and starts a lunchtime union group where workers teach each other AI tools.
S3.feel: Nervous but steadied by doing something.
S3.quote: If I can read the spec sheet and ask the AI what it really does, I can tell the union rep, actually, this still needs two operators.
S3.fieldNote: She blends personal advancement with collective power in an unusual way: learning AI so workers can check management's claims. The five-year window gives her a few good years and a cushion. She'd put off buying a home to stay mobile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and I'd want every worker to get paid training time, not just evenings after a ten-hour shift. I'd campaign for it. I'd also say out loud that the end point still needs a plan, because a decade of retraining doesn't help if there's nothing left to retrain for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally I think it's mostly good. I'd have years in maintenance, maybe move into installing robot lines for the supplier, earn properly for the first time. I just don't know what the last couple of years look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance course now and be on the robot cell within two years. Then I'd look at moving to the robot supplier or an automation company, even if it means a longer commute. I'd vote and campaign for a guaranteed income to kick in as jobs go, because I'd want it ready before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a small worry at the back about the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in campaigning for an income while expecting to do well yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but no, I don't think so. I've had no money my whole life, I know what it's like. Even if I'm alright, most people on my line won't be, and I'd be ashamed to climb up and pull the ladder after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 37-year-old you be doing, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably standing in some new factory with a laptop, teaching the robot where the boxes go. And then, I don't know, maybe teaching people. I think I'd like teaching.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a gift if workers get paid training time and would campaign for it. She'd also say openly that the end point still needs a plan.
S4.think: Personally she thinks it's mostly good: years in maintenance, maybe installing robot lines, and proper earnings for the first time. Only the last couple of years worry her.
S4.do: Starts the maintenance course now and aims to be on the robot cell within two years, then moves to a robot supplier or automation firm even with a longer commute. Votes and campaigns for a guaranteed income to start as jobs disappear.
S4.feel: Hopeful, with a small worry about the end.
S4.quote: I'd be ashamed to climb up and pull the ladder after me.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets her ambition and her politics sit together comfortably. She rejects the idea that doing well herself contradicts campaigning for others. A new hope surfaced at the end: teaching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The others give me time to climb, but that one pulls the ladder away while I'm still on the bottom rung. What would help is a guaranteed income straight away, and the company having to pay into a fund for anyone they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the training. Everyone talks about 'reskilling' like it's free and open. On my line it's been the boss's nephew. If the training goes to the same people as always, the robots won't be the problem, the old boys' club will be.

headlineQuote: If the training goes to the same people as always, the robots won't be the problem, the old boys' club will be.
portrait: Uma Nakamura is a 27-year-old packing line operator at a frozen pizza plant, ten months in and still calling the engineer more than she'd like. She teaches herself fault-finding with an AI chatbot every break and wants to become a maintenance technician for the robot lines. Steady change looks like her chance, while fast AGI breaks her plan and leaves her scared and cheated, though she quickly pivots to care shifts and organising. With five or ten years she sees good years ahead and still campaigns for a guaranteed income for others. Her sharpest anger is about who gets training, not about the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it pulls the ladder away while she's still on the bottom rung.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income straight away, and companies having to pay into a fund for anyone they replace.
